candidate.answerReason: Removing the two integer real zeros leaves a monic integer-coefficient quadratic. A nonreal root u+iv requires integer coefficients -2u and u²+v². Only A meets these conditions, and (x-1)(x-2)(x²-x+3) supplies a valid example.

methods.label: Examine the remaining quadratic
methods.explanation:
Factoring out the two integer real zeros leaves a monic quadratic \(Q(x)\) with integer coefficients. Indeed, division by a factor \(x-r\), where \(r\) is an integer, keeps the quotient coefficients integers: each long-division subtraction uses only integer coefficients.

Suppose a listed number \(z=u+iv\), with \(v\ne0\), is a zero of \(Q\). Because the coefficients are real, changing \(i\) to \(-i\) in the equation \(Q(z)=0\) shows that \(\overline z=u-iv\) is also a zero. These are distinct, so
\[
Q(x)=(x-z)(x-\overline z)
=x^2-2ux+(u^2+v^2).
\]
Both \(2u\) and \(u^2+v^2\) must therefore be integers.

For every choice, \(2u\) is an integer. The constant coefficients \(u^2+v^2\), however, are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{A}:&\quad \frac{1+11}{4}=3,\\
\mathrm{B}:&\quad \frac{1+1}{4}=\frac12,\\
\mathrm{C}:&\quad \frac14+1=\frac54,\\
\mathrm{D}:&\quad 1+\frac14=\frac54,\\
\mathrm{E}:&\quad \frac{1+13}{4}=\frac72.
\end{aligned}
\]
Only choice A gives an integer constant coefficient.

To establish that A really can occur, consider
\[
P(x)=(x-1)(x-2)(x^2-x+3).
\]
This is a monic quartic with integer coefficients. The quadratic has zeros \((1\pm i\sqrt{11})/2\), so the polynomial has exactly the two real zeros \(1\) and \(2\). Thus the answer is \(\boxed{\dfrac{1+i\sqrt{11}}{2}}\), choice \(\mathrm{A}\).

All choices have integral \(2u\), but their constant terms are 3, 1/2, 5/4, 5/4, and 7/2. Only A qualifies, and the constructed quartic verifies possibility with exactly two real integer zeros.
